es.summary: La deficiencia de hierro reduce la síntesis de hemoglobina, provocando anemia microcítica e hipocromica y disminución del transporte de oxígeno.
key_points: Los factores de riesgo incluyen menstruación abundante, embarazo y sangrado gastrointestinal.
Diagnóstico mediante CBC, ferritina y saturación de transferrina.
El tratamiento incluye suplementos de hierro oral y dieta rica en hierro.

pathophysiology: Ingesta o absorción insuficiente de hierro.
Disminuye la producción de hemoglobina en la médula ósea.
RBC microcíticas e hipocrómicas reducen la capacidad de transporte de O₂.
Hipoxia tisular estimula la eritropoyesis, pero sin hierro disponible la respuesta es limitada.
risk_factors: Dieta pobre en hierro (vegetariana sin suplementación).
Trastornos de absorción (celiaquía, enfermedad inflamatoria intestinal).
signs_symptoms: Uñas quebradizas (koiloniquia) y caída del cabello.
Pica (ansia por comer hielo o tierra).
diagnostics: Ferritina sérica <15 ng/mL (indicador de reservas de hierro).
Saturación de transferrina <20 % y capacidad total de fijación de hierro aumentada.
Frotis de sangre muestra eritrocitos microcíticos e hipocrómicos.
treatment: Suplementación oral de hierro (p. ej., sulfato ferroso).
Vitamina C (ácido ascórbico) para mejorar absorción.
Dieta rica en hierro hemo (carnes rojas, hígado) y no hemo (legumbres, espinaca).
Hierro intravenoso si intolerancia oral o necesidad de reposición rápida.
Transfusión de sangre si Hb <7 g/dL o síntomas graves.
complications: Insuficiencia cardíaca por aumento de la demanda circulatoria.
Disminución de la inmunidad y mayor riesgo de infecciones.
Complicaciones obstétricas (parto prematuro, bajo peso al nacer).
Retraso del crecimiento y desarrollo en niños.
nursing_care: Evaluar signos vitales y nivel de conciencia cada 4 h.
Monitorear hemoglobina y ferritina cada 2‑4 semanas.
Observar efectos adversos del hierro (náuseas, estreñimiento, heces negras).
Registrar ingesta de suplementos y alimentos ricos en hierro.
Promover posición semisentada para facilitar la respiración si hay disnea.
patient_teaching: Tomar el suplemento con agua y vitamina C, evitar té, café o lácteos cerca de la dosis.
Informar sobre posibles efectos gastrointestinales y cómo manejarlos.
Importancia de la adherencia al tratamiento durante al menos 3‑6 meses.
Incluir alimentos ricos en hierro en cada comida (carnes, legumbres, frutos secos).
Buscar atención médica si aparecen sangrados inusuales o empeora la fatiga.

en.summary: Iron deficiency reduces hemoglobin synthesis, causing microcytic hypochromic anemia and decreased oxygen transport.
key_points: Risk factors include heavy menstruation, pregnancy, and gastrointestinal bleeding.
Diagnosis via CBC, ferritin, and transferrin saturation.
Treatment includes oral iron supplements and iron‑rich diet.

pathophysiology: Decreases hemoglobin production in the bone marrow.
Microcytic, hypochromic RBCs reduce O₂ transport capacity.
Tissue hypoxia stimulates erythropoiesis, but limited iron restricts the response.
risk_factors: Absorption disorders (celiac disease, inflammatory bowel disease).
diagnostics: Serum ferritin <15 ng/mL (indicator of iron stores).
Transferrin saturation <20 % and increased total iron binding capacity.
Peripheral smear shows microcytic, hypochromic erythrocytes.
treatment: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) to improve absorption.
Diet rich in heme iron (red meats, liver) and non‑heme iron (legumes, spinach).
Intravenous iron if oral intolerance or rapid repletion needed.
Blood transfusion if Hb <7 g/dL or severe symptoms.]

outcomes: Energy level: increase to 4/5 on 0‑5 scale within 2 weeks
Ability to perform activities of daily living without exhaustion in 4 weeks

interventions.action: Assess energy level and activity tolerance each shift
interventions.rationale: Measures treatment response and guides care adjustments.

interventions.action: Administer prescribed oral iron supplement and record intake
interventions.rationale: Replaces iron deficit and improves hemoglobin production.

interventions.action: Educate patient on vitamin C importance for iron absorption
interventions.rationale: Optimizes oral supplement efficacy.

interventions.action: Monitor hemoglobin and ferritin every 2‑4 weeks
interventions.rationale: Confirms hematologic response to treatment.

interventions.action: Encourage iron‑rich diet and document food intake
interventions.rationale: Supports long‑term iron store replenishment.

care_plans.diagnosis: Risk for decreased cardiac tissue perfusion
outcomes: Blood pressure maintained >90/60 mmHg during hospitalization
Heart rate <100 bpm without sustained tachycardia

interventions.action: Monitor vital signs every 4 h, focusing on BP and HR
interventions.rationale: Detects early signs of hypoperfusion.

interventions.action: Assess level of consciousness and skin/mucous color
interventions.rationale: Clinical indicators of adequate perfusion.

interventions.action: Administer supplemental oxygen if SpO₂ <92 %
interventions.rationale: Improves oxygen saturation and reduces cardiac load.

interventions.action: Notify physician of any Hb drop <7 g/dL
interventions.rationale: Facilitates transfusion decisions to maintain perfusion.

interventions.action: Promote relative rest and avoid intense physical exertion
interventions.rationale: Reduces myocardial oxygen demand.

summary.0.quote: RBCs do not have adequate iron to fully form and are smaller than normal, indicating impaired Hb synthesis.

key_points.0.quote: Common causes include iron-deficiency anemia, thalassemia, and certain chronic diseases.

key_points.1.quote: Anemia can result from acute bleeding, as in trauma or surgery, or from chronic, low-level bleeding, as in gastrointestinal bleeding or heavy menstrual periods.

key_points.3.quote: Oral iron supplements may be taken up to three times a day with food to boost body stores of iron and promote appropriate production of RBCs.

sections.pathophysiology.0.quote: This disorder may develop from inadequate iron intake, impaired iron absorption (e.g., from celiac disease or weight-loss surgery), or increased iron loss (e.g., from menstruation or gastrointestinal bleeding) (Camaschella, 2019).

sections.risk_factors.1.quote: This disorder may develop from inadequate iron intake, impaired iron absorption (e.g., from celiac disease or weight-loss surgery), or increased iron loss (e.g., from menstruation or gastrointestinal bleeding) (Camaschella, 2019).

sections.risk_factors.3.quote: Anemia can result from acute bleeding, as in trauma or surgery, or from chronic, low-level bleeding, as in gastrointestinal bleeding or heavy menstrual periods.

sections.signs_symptoms.0.quote: Those affected by the disorder often experience debilitating symptoms including fatigue, weakness, pale skin tone, and shortness of breath.

sections.signs_symptoms.1.quote: Objective signs may include physical findings such as pale skin and mucus membranes and delayed capillary refill time.

sections.treatment.0.quote: These supplements may come in the form of ferrous sulfate, ferrous gluconate, or other iron preparations.

sections.treatment.5.quote: In more serious cases, the disorder can cause complications affecting the heart, brain, and other vital organs.

sections.treatment.7.quote: Apply nursing concepts and plan associated nursing care for the patient with anemia
